title: Two gardens
hookLine: a rich man boasts of his gardens, and they are ruined overnight (18:32–43)

cards: Two men. One owns two vineyards, hedged around with date palms, fields of grain between them, a stream running through the middle. Both gardens bear fruit and hold nothing back.
The other man has much less. The rich man starts talking to his friend, and then walks into his garden, still talking. Al-Kahf calls this a parable, a story set out as an example.
Today: what he says in that garden, and what his friend says back.

teach.h: MORE THAN YOU. IT WILL NEVER END.
teach.b: The rich man says three things, each going further. First: I have more than you in wealth, and more people behind me. That's comparison.
Then, walking into his garden, wronging himself, he says: I don't think this will ever perish.
That's permanence. Then: I don't think the Hour will ever come, and even if I'm brought back to my Lord, I'll find something better there. That's entitlement.
His friend doesn't mock him. He answers: do you deny the One who made you from dust?

And then the line this day is built on, in Pickthall's translation: "If only, when thou enteredst thy garden, thou hadst said: That which Allah willeth (will come to pass)! There is no strength save in Allah!"
In Arabic: ma sha' Allah, la quwwata illa billah. What God wills; there is no power except through God.

teach.h: INSHALLAH FOR PLANS, MASHALLAH FOR GIFTS.
teach.b: Inshallah, if God wills, is said about the future. Mashallah, what God has willed, is said about what's already here. One is for plans, the other for blessings.
Then the story ends quickly. The fruit is struck.
The man stands wringing his hands over everything he spent on it, the vines collapsed on their trellises, and says: I wish I had not set anything beside my Lord.

teach.h: THERE IS NO STRENGTH SAVE IN ALLAH!
teach.b: Today mashallah is said when admiring something, a new baby, a friend's house, a child's grades, and some say it as protection against envy.
But in al-Kahf its first job is simpler: to remember, out loud, whose the garden was.

how: Muslims say mashallah when admiring a blessing, their own or someone else's, often adding la quwwata illa billah; some also say it to ward off envy.

o: the paradise promised to the patient and grateful
a contest between two kings over a field
a parable of a rich man who forgot whose it was

games.q: inside the parable — tap the pairs.

s: the friend mocks the rich man
he answers seriously: do you deny the One who made you from dust?
mashallah and inshallah mean the same thing
inshallah is if God wills, about the future; mashallah is what God has willed, about what's here.
the rich man ends by regretting he set anything beside his Lord
18:42: he wrings his hands and says he wishes he hadn't.

games.q: your friend walks you through his vineyards, boasting they'll never perish. you have far less. what do you say, in the parable?
o: if only you'd said: what God wills; there is no power except through God.
games.why: the friend gives him the words he should have said on entering the garden (18:39). by the next verses, the fruit is gone.

practice: Walk slowly through your own garden in your mind: a home, a skill, a body that works, children, a paycheck, a reputation.

At each thing, pause; if you're Muslim, you can say mashallah, la quwwata illa billah, and if not, simply notice that you didn't make this alone. Then stay with whatever feeling comes, gratitude, or worry about losing it.

wordCard.voice: Two gardens. A parable of a man who said his blessings would never end, and the friend who told him what he should have said. Today's word.

orig.s: مَا شَاءَ ٱللَّهُ لَا قُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِٱللَّه
orig.say: maa SHAA-'al-laah, laa QUW-wa-ta IL-laa bil-LAAH
orig.note: Arabic: what God has willed; there is no power except through God (18:39).

carryVoice: Your line: mashallah, no power but his. The garden was always on loan. Day four hundred sixty-seven, done.
